Serialise a bitmap

Source: R/serial.R
roar_serialize.Rd

roar_serialize() writes x in the portable Roaring format, the one that the C, C++, Java, Go, Rust and Python implementations share, as a raw vector. roar_unserialize() reads such bytes back into a 32-bit bitmap and roar64_unserialize() into a zuroar64. The two formats share no marker that tells them apart, so the caller chooses the reader; it is never guessed from the bytes.

Usage

roar_serialize(x, optimize = FALSE)

roar_unserialize(bytes, trailing = c("error", "ignore"))

roar64_unserialize(bytes, trailing = c("error", "ignore"))

Arguments

x

A bitmap.

optimize

If TRUE, write run-length containers wherever they are smaller, from an optimised copy; x itself is not changed.

bytes

A raw vector holding a portable bitmap: 32-bit for roar_unserialize(), 64-bit for roar64_unserialize().

trailing

What to do with bytes after the end of the bitmap: "error", the default, or "ignore".

Value

roar_serialize() a raw vector, roar_unserialize() a zuroar and roar64_unserialize() a zuroar64.

Details

A bitmap also survives saveRDS(), serialize() and a trip to another R process on its own, through the same format. Use roar_serialize() for bytes that other programs, or other Roaring libraries, will read.

roar_unserialize() treats its input as untrusted. It checks the length the header claims, reads with CRoaring's bounded deserialiser, which never reads past the end, and validates the result, so corrupt or hostile bytes give a zuroar_error_format error rather than a crash.

See also

roar_size() for the number of bytes roar_serialize() writes.

Examples

x <- roar(c(1, 5, 9, 100000))
b <- roar_serialize(x)
b
#>  [1] 3a 30 00 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 02 00 01 00 00 00 18 00 00 00 1e 00 00 00 01
#> [26] 00 05 00 09 00 a0 86
roar_unserialize(b)
#> <zuroar> 4 values in [1, 100000]: 1 5 9 100000

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".roar")
writeBin(roar_serialize(x), path)
roar_unserialize(readBin(path, "raw", file.size(path)))
#> <zuroar> 4 values in [1, 100000]: 1 5 9 100000
